entries.body: The first of the beings created by the "First Ancestral Race" long before humanity; the Angels are described as Adam's offspring. A contact experiment on Adam is what triggered Second Impact.

links.label: Adam vs. Lilith, precisely which is which
The two artificial cavities tied to Adam's and Lilith's arrival

quote.original: 第1使徒　アダム　使徒を生み出した生命の起源の一つ。セカンドインパクトを引き起こした。
quote.translation: "1st Angel: Adam — one of the two origins of life that gave rise to the Angels. Triggered Second Impact."

entries.title: What was First Impact?
entries.body: Referenced as the event that shaped the Earth long before Second Impact, tied to Adam and Lilith's arrival. Different tie-in material describes it differently, and the TV series itself barely touches it.

entries.scene: Fuyutsuki is pressed on what Gendo is really after
entries.title: Gendo as tragic rather than purely villainous
entries.body: Gendo's plan is explicitly framed here as wanting to be with Yui again, but how much sympathy that deserves given the harm he causes Shinji and everyone around him to get there is a matter of ongoing viewer disagreement rather than something the text adjudicates for you.

links.label: Back to Gendo's introduction
How that read Gendo from the very first episode
How Gendo and Yui's relationship actually started

entries.scene: Misato takes Shinji down into Terminal Dogma
entries.title: Lilith
entries.body: A being of the same origin as Adam, kept crucified and sealed in NERV's Terminal Dogma. The Lilin — i.e., humanity — are described as descended from Lilith rather than Adam, and Lilith's flesh and soul are the source material for the Evangelions and for Rei.

links.label: Her connection to Rei
Which of these two is which, again?
The other artifact kept in the same chamber
The scene where Kaji first shows her off, misidentified
The Spear being pulled out of her and fired at the Moon

entries.title: Adam/Lilith identity mix-ups across versions
entries.body: Which being is sealed in Terminal Dogma, which one Gendo's faction actually possesses, and which one the embryo NERV keeps separately is called is inconsistent enough between the TV series, supplementary material, and later reprints that fans still debate the "correct" mapping. Some treat this as evidence of a deliberately unresolved cosmology rather than a continuity error.

entries.title: Kaji is killed
entries.body: Kaji is killed off-screen in this episode, having gotten too close to the truth about Adam, Lilith, and Instrumentality he'd spent the series digging into. Who specifically killed him (SEELE or Gendo's own faction) is left unstated.

links.label: Back to Kaji's introduction
The later edit that confirms who actually did it

quote.original: 一方、廃人状態であったアスカは目を覚まし...（第22話の文脈で加持がその死の直前まで調査を続けていたことが描かれる）
quote.translation: "Meanwhile Asuka, who had been catatonic, awakens..." (the episode's synopsis places Kaji's death here, mid-way through NERV's occupation crisis, after his investigation into NERV's secrets)

entries.scene: The mass-production Evangelions are activated
entries.title: How much of a person is in a dummy plug
entries.body: The dummy plug is described as simulating a pilot's mental patterns rather than containing a true digitized soul, but the mass-production Evas' dummy plugs are built from Kaworu specifically, and their on-screen behavior (screaming, bleeding) reads as more than simulation. How much of that is meant literally is left to the viewer.

links.label: The Kaworu these are built from

entries.title: The Rei clones
entries.body: A tank of spare Rei bodies is kept in Terminal Dogma; when a given Rei dies, another takes her place, personality and memory carried over to a degree the show never fully explains.

links.label: Whether that's really "her"

entries.title: Lilith's soul divided across Rei and Unit-00
entries.body: Building on a scene in The End of Evangelion where Rei is welcomed "home" by Lilith, a popular theory holds that souls in this universe are divisible, and that a fragment of Lilith's soul persists in each Rei clone and possibly in Unit-00 itself (offered as one explanation for Unit-00's own unexplained hostile incidents). This is an inference from a handful of suggestive scenes, not a stated rule.

links.label: The scene this theory is built on
The earliest hint of this, well before it's explained

entries.title: Do the Rei clones share one continuous identity?
entries.body: Each Rei carries the prior one's memories to some extent, but the show never states whether that makes her the same person, a new person with inherited memories, or something in between — the question is posed to the audience more than once and never answered for them.

entries.title: Kaworu Nagisa
entries.body: Arrives late in the story as a new pilot candidate, forms an immediate bond with Shinji, and is then revealed to be an Angel in human form, sent by SEELE to reach Lilith in Terminal Dogma. Shinji is left to decide whether to kill him.

links.label: What he actually felt
Is he really an Angel, though?

entries.title: What Kaworu actually felt for Shinji
entries.body: Kaworu tells Shinji he loves him within a day of meeting him, then lets Shinji kill him rather than fight back. Whether this is genuine affection an Angel is nonetheless capable of, a calculated move to complete his mission, or both at once, is never resolved — the scene is written to support any of the three.

entries.title: Is Kaworu an Angel, in exactly the same sense the others are?
entries.body: Kaworu is called the Seventeenth Angel but presents as fully human and self-aware in a way none of the others do, and material outside the original TV run has described his origin differently. The TV series itself leaves the discrepancy alone.

entries.scene: The episode's Japanese title
entries.title: The title "最後のシ者" is a pun
entries.body: The Japanese title for this episode splits the kanji in Kaworu's surname, Nagisa (渚), into its component radicals and re-renders one as the katakana シ, so the title reads as "the last シ者" — deliberately ambiguous between 使者 ("messenger," SEELE's errand for Kaworu) and 死者 ("the dead," what he becomes by the end of it).

links.label: The Kaworu this refers to

quote.original: 「シ者」は、渚カヲルの「渚」の偏と旁を分けたもの。使者、あるいは死者。
quote.translation: "'シ者' is formed by splitting the radical and phonetic components of Kaworu Nagisa's surname kanji, 渚. [It reads ambiguously as] 使者 ('messenger'), or 死者 ('the dead')."

entries.title: Acceptance vs. rejection of Instrumentality
entries.body: A common reading pairs the TV finale and The End of Evangelion as two sides of the same choice: the TV ending shows Shinji arriving at self-acceptance from inside a dissolved, unified consciousness, while EoE shows the same decision played out physically — Shinji ultimately rejecting total union with others in favor of a painful but individual existence. Neither film states this framing outright; it's inferred from how the two versions rhyme.

links.label: Why there are two endings at all
How EoE actually plays it out

entries.scene: The finale breaks into congratulatory character-actor cutaways
entries.title: The finale as commentary on Anno's own depression
entries.body: Director Hideaki Anno has spoken about depression during the show's production, and the TV finale's abrupt turn toward real-world footage, character-actor congratulations, and direct address to the viewer is widely read as breaking the fourth wall on purpose — a message about escapism versus engaging with a difficult reality, layered on top of Shinji's in-story arc rather than replacing it. Sociologist Miyadai Shinji has argued the series itself started as a lighter, more conventional "school anime" concept and drifted toward this ending as production wore on and the director's own state of mind changed.

links.label: The same self-scrutiny, voiced during episode 1

quote.original: 庵野は「人間ドラマは頭の中で考えてもできないので、仕方なく自分をドラマにそのまま投影しており、『エヴァ』のキャラは全部自分自身だというのはそういう意味だ」と語っている。
quote.translation: "Anno has said: 'I can't write human drama just by thinking it up in my head, so I end up projecting myself directly into the drama instead — that's what I mean when I say every character in Eva is really myself.'"

entries.title: "I mustn't run away" becomes "it's okay to run away"
entries.body: Shinji's early refrain — "I mustn't run away" (逃げちゃダメだ) — is the closest thing the show has to a stated thesis in its first half. By the finale it's been replaced with the opposite: it's okay to run away. Character designer Yoshiyuki Sadamoto is credited with suggesting the shift.

quote.original: 物語開始直後に「逃げちゃダメだ」と言っていたのが、最後に「逃げてもいい」に変わったのは、貞本のアドバイスによる。
quote.translation: "That the line 'I mustn't run away,' spoken right at the story's start, changed to 'it's okay to run away' by the end, came from [character designer Yoshiyuki] Sadamoto's suggestion."

entries.title: Why did the finale turn out this way? Even the staff disagree
entries.body: The standard explanation is that production had fallen catastrophically behind — only around a third of the episodes were fully animated by the time the show started airing, and the two finale episodes were assembled largely from recycled footage out of necessity. But several staff accounts complicate that: magazine editor Ogura Yuichiro says the finale's plot points were already locked in by January 1996, two months before broadcast; GAINAX president Yamaga Hiroyuki says the show was never so broken it couldn't have been finished conventionally; and assistant director Tsurumaki Kazuya has said Anno had "a chance of winning" with this ending in mind from the start, and considered the backlash itself part of that win — a show forgotten in six months was the actual failure state he was avoiding. Anno himself maintains the finale was always intended to be exactly this, schedule aside, aiming at what he called "liberation from cel animation."

links.label: The other ending this led to

quote.original: 鶴巻和哉は「第25、26話も庵野監督なりに勝算があってやっている...本当はもっと早い段階で種明かしのネタを全部考えてシナリオを書いちゃうのが一番楽なんですよ。でも庵野監督はそれでは楽しすぎだとか思ったんでしょう」と証言している。
quote.translation: "Tsurumaki Kazuya has testified: 'Episodes 25 and 26 were made with director Anno believing, in his own way, that he had a chance of winning... The easiest thing would really have been to work out every twist far earlier and just write the script. But I think Director Anno felt that would have been too easy, or too enjoyable, [to be the right choice].'"

entries.title: The original plan had 28 Angels, not 17
entries.body: Early planning documents describe 28 Angels rather than the 17 the finished show uses, with a climax involving a second wave of 12 Angels descending from the moon alongside Instrumentality's activation. That structural role — a large final wave of antagonists tied to Instrumentality — survives in the finished work in a different form: the nine Mass-Production Evangelions that SEELE deploys near the end.

quote.original: 使徒の数が17体ではなく28体であったり、物語のクライマックスでの12使徒との戦いや人類補完計画の発動が含まれていた。
quote.translation: "The number of Angels was 28 rather than 17, and the story's climax was to include a battle against 12 Angels alongside the activation of the Human Instrumentality Project."

entries.title: The wholly-new film that never got made
entries.body: The original 1996 plan was for both replacement final episodes to be an entirely new theatrical film, not a clip-show. Production fell too far behind again; at a February 1997 press conference — one month before the planned release — Anno publicly apologized, and the all-new film was scrapped. What released instead split into two films: a clip-show-plus-new-footage recap (Death (True)²) and then the genuinely new Air/まごころを、君に in July 1997. The original all-new concept became what Japanese sources call a "phantom project" (幻の企画) — never produced in that form.

quote.original: 劇場版の制作が大幅に遅れ、公開1か月前の1997年2月14日に緊急記者会見が開かれた。席上で、庵野秀明総監督が謝罪を行い...同じく夏に公開が予定されていた「完全新作の劇場版」は幻の企画となってしまった。
quote.translation: "Production of the theatrical film fell drastically behind, and an emergency press conference was held on February 14, 1997, one month before release. At it, general director Hideaki Anno apologized... the 'wholly new theatrical film' also planned for that summer became a phantom project."

entries.title: Concepts from the scrapped all-new film
entries.body: Never filmed, so not part of any released continuity — but Anno has described draft ideas from the abandoned all-new film: pilots merging directly with an Evangelion's "womb" rather than using an entry plug, requiring a C-section-like extraction under a strict time limit (missing it meant the pilot's literal death), and Angels that prey on and consume people outright. Anno has noted the latter idea predates, and reads similarly to, Attack on Titan's premise by well over a decade.

links.label: Why this film was never made

quote.original: 「パイロットはエントリープラグを使わずにEVAの子宮に直接入って一体化する」という表現を考えていたという。そして出るときは摘出手術をする。また「タイムリミットがあり、間に合わない場合は取り込まれて『人としては』死んでしまう」という設定だったという。
quote.translation: "They had considered depicting pilots merging directly with an Evangelion's womb without using an entry plug. Getting out again would require a surgical extraction. There was also said to be a time limit — missing it meant being absorbed and dying 'as a human being.'"

entries.title: Two different endings exist
entries.body: The TV series' original episodes 25–26, made under a tightened budget, resolve the story almost entirely inside Shinji's own psyche. The End of Evangelion (1997), a theatrical film, was written and produced afterward as an alternate, effects-driven ending depicting Third Impact's events directly — both are considered canon, telling the same climax from different angles.

links.label: One way to read the pair together

entries.title: Third Impact
entries.body: The series' climax: the event that carries out (or nearly carries out) Human Instrumentality. What actually happens, and how much of it is undone by the end, differs between the TV series' final two episodes and the alternate ending in The End of Evangelion.

entries.scene: Rei III dissolves into Lilith: "I'm home." / "Welcome home."
entries.title: Rei's reunion with Lilith
entries.body: In The End of Evangelion, Rei III is shown reuniting with Lilith with the words "I'm home," and Lilith replying "Welcome home" — one of the few moments the show gestures directly at what Rei actually is.

entries.scene: The final shot, on the beach
entries.title: What actually happens on the beach at the end of EoE
entries.body: The final shot — Shinji strangling, then stopping, Asuka, who touches his cheek and says "kimochi warui" ("disgusting" / "I feel sick") — is one of anime's most argued-over endings. Readings range from a literal moment between two survivors of a mostly-undone Third Impact, to a purely symbolic beat with no fixed literal status, to a bleak coda implying nothing is resolved. The film gives no voiceover or text to settle it.

links.label: What state the rest of the world is in

entries.title: A cyclical/recurring Third Impact
entries.body: Some fans read hints across the franchise (including the later Rebuild films, which explicitly restart the story after a Third Impact) as evidence that impacts recur in cycles rather than the original TV/EoE story being a one-off — though the original series itself makes no such claim; this reading leans heavily on later material re-interpreted backward.

entries.title: What state is the world actually in after The End of Evangelion?
entries.body: The final scene shows Shinji and Asuka alone on a wrecked shoreline. Whether this is a reversed, near-total, or partial Third Impact — and whether anyone else survived it — is left to the audience.
